title: Choosing a practice
hook: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame

segments.voice: Yesterday, closed practices, and your line: not mine to take. Did you hear a community tell its own story, in its own words? Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

A shoe store, a Saturday afternoon. The runner on the bench has tried on six pairs. One pair is beautiful and pinches. One is what a famous athlete wears and slides off the heel. The salesperson finally says something useful: walk to the back of the store and back, and tell me which one you forget you're wearing. After weeks of visiting the world's schools of practice, a fair question is waiting. Which of these, if any, would you actually wear every day? Not the most impressive. Not the one a friend swears by. The one that fits. Today is a way of asking that question with care.
screen: `SIX PAIRS ON THE BENCH.` → `THE ONE YOU FORGET YOU'RE WEARING.` → `WHICH WOULD YOU WEAR DAILY?`

segments.voice: Four questions, each worth slowing down for. The first is fit. Does this practice suit your body, your temperament, your days? Someone with a bad knee may not sit cross-legged for an hour. Someone who thinks best while moving might find a walking practice or slow movement easier than stillness. Someone who loves words may be drawn to reading and reflection. Fit isn't laziness. A practice you can actually keep beats a grand one you abandon. The second is a good teacher. Not a famous one: one who has done the practice for a long time, who is honest about its limits, and who welcomes your questions. The third is community. Practice is easier in company, and company keeps you honest. A group that sits together, sings together or studies together will notice when you stop showing up. The fourth is an ethical frame. Several schools on this tour came with one: precepts, commandments, virtues, vows. A technique without a way of living around it can drift. Two old texts give a way to test all four. In the Buddhist Kalama Sutta, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells a group of confused villagers not to go by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone, but to notice for themselves which things lead to harm and which to well-being, and to choose accordingly. And in the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus gives a short test for telling true prophets from false: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." Each text speaks in its own setting, and each asks you to watch what a practice actually grows in a person, over time.
screen: `FIT: BODY, TEMPERAMENT, DAYS.` · `A TEACHER WHO WELCOMES QUESTIONS.` · `COMPANY KEEPS YOU HONEST.` · `AN ETHICAL FRAME AROUND IT.` · then, large: `KNOW THEM BY THEIR FRUITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: list what you need. Settle, and breathe. Take the four questions one by one, slowly. What fits your body and your days, right now, not in some ideal year? What would you want from a teacher? Do you need company to keep going, or quiet? And what way of living would you want a practice to sit inside? You don't have to answer well. Let one honest word come for each. The bell holds the time.
Choosing a practice. Four questions: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame, tested by what the practice grows in a person. Today's word.
Your line: what fits. Today, write down your four words somewhere you'll see them again, a note on your phone or a slip in your wallet. Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: People choosing a practice often try several, look for a teacher with long experience who welcomes questions, join a group that practices together, and keep the practice inside an ethical frame such as precepts, commandments or vows; in some traditions a newcomer simply starts by attending and asking.

trapdoor: what you thought: choosing a practice means finding the most powerful one.
what it means: asking four questions, fit, teacher, community and ethics, and choosing what you can actually keep.
what a scholar hears: the Kalama Sutta's test is not belief but results: what leads to harm, what leads to well-being, noticed for yourself.

notes: The Kalama Sutta is paraphrased. Confirm the numbering (AN 3.65) and that the paraphrase (not going by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone; noticing what leads to harm and to well-being) is fair, and not stretched into a general license to ignore tradition.
Matthew 7:16 is quoted from the KJV; in context Jesus is speaking of false prophets. The script calls it 'a short test for teachers', which a Christian reviewer should confirm is fair.
The script says 'Several schools on this tour came with' an ethical frame, referring to the path's own Block F days.
The four questions come from the index line. No claim is made about which practice suits whom; the examples (bad knee, thinking while moving, loving words) are illustrative only.
Editor pass: Matthew 7:16 now framed as a test for telling true prophets from false, as in its context, not 'a test for teachers'.
